title: Loss functions
outcome: By the end, I can explain loss functions using a traced example and a stated limitation.
scenario: Compare candidate losses with the same targets and denominator.
given: Targets [1, 3]; A predicts [0, 4]; B predicts [1, 5]. Use MSE over both cases.
All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

steps.label: Compare objective
steps.detail: A wins under MSE; both MAEs equal1.

explanation: For this loss calculation, the signed error is prediction minus target. MSE squares each error before averaging; MAE takes its absolute value. A spreads its error equally across both cases, while B concentrates it in one case. Squaring makes the larger individual error count more. State the objective before selecting a model, because these two objectives give different comparisons.

counterfactual.change: Choose MAE instead of MSE as the sole criterion.
counterfactual.prediction: A and B tie at MAE1.
counterfactual.reason: Squared error penalises B’s concentrated error more, while absolute errors both sum 2.

student_task: Why must the report name the chosen loss? Point to the relevant step in the picture, then write the changed result and the rule or evidence that supports it.
teacher_answer: The same predictions produce a strict A win under MSE and a tie under MAE; “better” depends on the declared objective. Changed-case check: A and B tie at MAE1. Squared error penalises B’s concentrated error more, while absolute errors both sum 2.
project_evidence: For your Image-pattern Network Investigation, save the input, procedure, observed result and limitation of this check. Label this worked example as practice; use a different, previously unreviewed case when checking independent understanding.
limits: Training loss is not automatically a held-out performance estimate or a complete measure of use consequences.
